item.title: Honoring Who You Are While Growing
item.description:
Self-Esteem

Honoring Who You Are While Growing

Apprenticeship begins where self-worth and change coexist.

Posted July 26, 2026

Key points
  • It is unnecessary to turn against yourself in order to grow.
  • It's important to understand personal growth as an ongoing welcome to parts of yourself.
  • Practice honoring who you are now while opening to further development.
Source: Greg Rosenke/Unsplash

Initially, any reference to growth only pertained to plants and animals. In the 15th century, growth was defined as a person’s body parts and height. It wasn’t until the early 20th century that the notion of growth or maturation came to be applied to human psychology. One way to think of a person’s personal psychological growth is as change that enhances our capacities to think, feel, and act. We can consider thinking to be flourishing when we are accepting of ambiguity and able to distinguish our stories about people and events from the reality of people and events. It means being clear about our biases and maintaining curiosity.

Emotional growth occurs when we can accept the full range of our emotions, name them, and talk about them. We allow physical sensations in the body to point us toward emotional energy, allowing us to distinguish emotions from ideas. Our behavior matures when we are clear about our intentions and able to identify and act on what is within our control. It also means identifying which behavior is in our best interest and which action serves others. Growth is reflected in our ability to take responsibility for our choices rather than blaming others. Growth often begins with something we desire, like having more effective boundaries, living with more compassion and empathy, and greater clarity about what we value. Of course, it helps to identify your internal resources, such as prioritizing and remaining focused. Also, resilience and patience in some areas of learning call for a devoted apprenticeship. And there are external resources, such as workshops, books, classes, and teachers who might specialize in your area of interest.

Two Paths to Growth

The first is really a non-path to growth. It sounds like, “I’m good with who I am now, and I have no need to pursue change.” This is a developmental dead-end. It is typically motivated by fear. One fear of change is that it may suggest there’s something wrong with me now. The second fear is that further self-exploration might reveal a hidden shortcoming.

The second path is “I really need to change because I am quite damaged.” This is a common approach to growth. It is motivated by shame and championed by many vendors of personal growth. The pitch sounds like, “You’re substandard now, but with my guidance and/or my product, you’ll be a better person.” It’s packaged in a variety of ways, and it sells, confirming our inadequacy and promises of redemption.

The Paradoxical Path

A paradox brings together two things that do not seem to go together, or that appear contradictory. The paradoxical path brings acceptance of who we are now together with a desire to develop. I was first introduced to a paradoxical developmental model by Sheldon Kopp in his book, The Hanged Man. Kopp wrote, “I’m no longer interested in character development as long as that implies in any way that my Buddhahood is not already at hand.” Let’s unpack this quote. We can understand the word “Buddhahood” as Kopp’s essential worth as a human being. We can say that Kopp is not interested in character development if that implies that his essential worth is not already present. The implication is that he would be interested in character development if the process begins by affirming he is essentially fine the way he is.

Hence, we face a paradox when we claim our present worth and seek further development. I think of further development as a welcome to some part of ourselves. The act of welcoming needs to continue throughout our lives. There is no arrival. Someone in you awaits your welcome. Every welcome simply initiates a new apprenticeship. It may be that we face an old learning in a deeper way. We can bring more depth to our loving, an ability to let go, a capacity for acceptance, as well as new dimensions of courage and freedom.

I continue to employ the paradoxical developmental model in both my personal and professional lives. There is something deeply liberating about sitting with new clients, reminding them that they are the best versions of themselves on the planet, with welcomes, apprenticeships, discoveries, and adventures to come.

item.title: Why Due Dates Motivate Progress and How to Benefit From Them
item.description:
Procrastination

Why Due Dates Motivate Progress and How to Benefit From Them

Five simple steps to overcome creative procrastination and finally finish art.

Posted July 26, 2026

Key points
  • Creative projects often stall without a meaningful deadline.
  • One finished project can replace years of unnecessary guilt.
  • Small actions build momentum better than waiting for motivation.

When my son, Aaron, and daughter-in-law, Lizzie, moved back to Massachusetts in August of 2020, they brought with them their furniture, small appliances, clothes, and a stack of T-shirts. Lizzie had been collecting these wearable mementos since kindergarten. She had bags of them. Each shirt told a story. Each one served as a touchpoint for a day, a membership, a passage through childhood.

As a sewist, I suggested, “I could make you a T-shirt quilt.”

“That would be awesome,” Lizzie said. Being a scientist, she quickly created neatly folded stacks—each one representing a theme. Girl Scouts, band, Boy Scouts (she met my son through its then co-ed Explorers program), theater productions, trips around the world, and of course a few miscellaneous, un-categorizable shirts.

There were 76 shirts in all.

The next action fell squarely on me.

I did what a lot of creatives do when faced with a large project. I did nothing. Well, that’s not entirely true. I ruminated on the task. I watched several YouTube videos. I bought the required supplies: batting, bias tape, fusible interfacing. I placed everything in a clear plastic bag, and I pushed the stacks aside for six years.

It’s not that I didn’t think about Lizzie’s T-shirt quilt. I did. At first, often. And then, less often, and then, I re-arranged my sewing supplies and worked on other projects instead. Things that had specific due dates. A new dress to wear to a concert. Projects for clients. Birthday presents to give away.

Last summer, Aaron and Lizzie relocated to the Midwest. They once again packed their belongings and now their pooch, Nox. Lizzie’s T-shirts remained behind with me.

I call these unfinished tasks ghost projects. They haunt you. When you least expect it, they grip you with a fear that you’re "not good enough." They whisper names like "quitter" or "serial procrastinator."

About six weeks ago, Lizzie informed us that she’d be returning to Massachusetts to host a bridal shower weekend for a friend. She planned to arrive on a Thursday, stay overnight, and then head out for the weekend at a coastal Airbnb.

That’s when the stars aligned. Suddenly, after six years, I had a due date. I had renewed focus and energy. A clear raison d’etre.

This fuel is nothing new or different for me. I have intentionally used a deadline as motivation before.

I named this motivational framework The B.R.A.I.D. CompassTM because a compass helps you navigate and find your direction. The letters stand for five simple steps: begin, reflect, act, invite, and deliver.

B: Begin Before You're Ready

As soon as you have a creative idea, get started. Begin before you have all the supplies and resources. Begin before you know how to proceed because makers often discover their next step only when they are in the middle of the project.

R: Reflect on What Matters

After you begin, take a moment, an hour, a day, or a week and reflect.

Ask yourself: What am I doing? Why?

Think about who will receive your product. (And it’s perfectly fine if you are the recipient of the make.)

A: Act in the Present Moment

Take an action—any action—toward progressing on the project.

I like to set a timer for 20 minutes. This quick sprint is often just the jumpstart to get the ball rolling.

Act on the project. And then, keep acting.

How do you stay motivated? See the next step.

I: Invite Others Into the Journey

When you invite someone to receive your work, decide on a time and a place. Be specific. This element solidifies and strengthens your efforts. Imagining an audience for your work intensifies your focus and attention and externalizes your labors.

In my case, Lizzie did not know about my intention to give her the finished quilt but aligning the due date with her planned arrival made all the difference, nonetheless.

D: Deliver the item

We all know that feeling when you’re going to host a dinner or a party. Knowing that others will be coming into your home, you see your surroundings differently. You notice the toothpaste spatters on the mirror. You notice the crumbs on the carpet. You notice the messy kitchen counter.

Sharing the due date activates all your senses to ramp up your efforts and cram as much work time as possible into your now limited schedule. You will figure out a way to deliver the art even if you find yourself sweating the last stitches, the last words, hoping for the paint to dry.

The Quilt, the Smile, the Relief

When Lizzie arrived at our house that Thursday evening, I pointed to a large cardboard box. My family gathered as we eagerly watched her open the box.

When Lizzie realized her long-anticipated t-shirt quilt was finished, she beamed with joy. We all shared in that delightful moment. And I felt a sense of relief and pride having completed this project.

Is your creativity confounded by a lack of focus?

Try This: BRAID Your Next Creative Project

  • Use the B.R.A.I.D. CompassTM to navigate your progress: begin, reflect, act, invite, deliver.
  • Choose one unfinished "ghost project" from your graveyard of partially complete work and begin.
  • Pause for a moment to think and reflect on the project, the steps, and the recipient.
  • Set a timer for 20 minutes today and take one action step.
  • Decide a real due date and put it on your calendar and then tell at least one person about your project and invite them to witness the finished result.
  • Deliver the product.

Creativity may be born from inspiration but learning how to navigate like a ship’s captain can be very powerful. And even if you’re just trying to find your way through an ocean of T-shirt pieces, a compass can help you stay on course. Picturing the smiles and gratitude of the lucky recipients will go a long way to boost your own confidence and complete the job.
